The instrument uses the mouth cavity as its resonating chamber, and the timbre is adjusted by changing the shape of the mouth and the position of the tongue; the range is comparatively limited but expressive. Its tone is both sharp and warm, unlike the linear quality of a conventional flute, and has a certain spring and lilt. When played the volume is relatively soft, yet it can be clearly picked out in an ensemble. Compared with the harmonica the khomus is sharper and carries a national character; compared with traditional lutes its sound is lighter and more nimble. The resonance relies mainly on the natural cavity of the vocal tract, which gives it a warm, voice-like quality, and it suits the folk music of the Turkic peoples of Central Asia.

Whether the tongue is of another material, and the materials of the frame and other parts, are not recorded in the source. The instrument is unrelated in form and structure to the three-string fretless lute, the komuz, though the name has the same origin; jaw harps of the same kind are also found in the music of Turkic-speaking peoples such as the Sakha and the Tuvans.

The earliest known instruments of the komuz kind date from the fourth century; the Azerbaijani gopuz is thought, on the evidence of a clay tablet image, to go back some six thousand years, and in the 1960s American archaeologists found near Jighamish in Iranian Azerbaijan a clay tablet showing a musician holding a similar instrument. The Book of Dede Korkut mentions the gopuz of Gorcha. The instrument is also found in Yakut and Tuvan music, and was carried into Hungary by the Cumans. Twenty Kyrgyz girls once played it together at the Moscow Bolshoi Theatre, and Zataevich notated it in two or three parts.

The temir komuz (sometimes called the iron komus, the jaw-harp komus or the gubuz) is a Kyrgyz jaw harp, while the komus is a three-string fretless lute. As an instrument, the temir komus is unrelated in style and structure to the komus; its name, however, comes from another popular Turkic instrument. The string komus is used by the Turkic peoples of Central Asia, such as the Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, Kazakhs, Turkmens and the Uyghurs, as well as by Azerbaijanis, Turks and Yakuts.
